recommendations.title: RECOMMENDATIONS
rec.reuseportOff.title: Multi-core socket sharing is disabled
rec.reuseportOff.body: Running with a single accept-queue socket. With {{cores}} cores available you are leaving significant throughput on the table. Enable multi-core socket sharing (turn on the reuseport option or run more than one worker) to use all cores — estimated gain: {{gain}}% more RPS.
rec.coreCount.title: Running workers < CPU cores
rec.coreCount.body: {{cores}} CPU cores detected but fewer workers are active. Each idle core is capacity you are not using. Increase the worker count to match available cores for maximum throughput.
rec.clockBound.title: CPU clock speed is the bottleneck
rec.clockBound.body: SHA-256 score ({{score}} MH/s) is below the 18 MH/s reference. This is per-core throughput; the most common cause of a very low score is NO hardware SHA acceleration (SHA-NI / ARMv8 crypto) — typical inside a VM/container that doesn't expose CPU crypto extensions — not raw clock speed. On bare metal with hardware SHA it is ~10× higher. Capacity projections (which scale this per-core number by core count) will be pessimistic here; on real hardware they will be much higher.
rec.tlsModerate.title: TLS full-handshake capacity is moderate
rec.tlsModerate.body: Estimated TLS handshake capacity: {{rps}}/s. Under heavy TLS loads consider session resumption (tickets / OCSP stapling) to reduce full-handshake pressure.
rec.http2.title: HTTP/2 multiplexing improves effective throughput
rec.http2.body: These estimates assume one request per connection. Real-world throughput with HTTP/2 clients can be significantly higher because many requests share the same TLS session, amortising handshake cost.
rec.calibration.title: Calibration caveat
rec.calibration.fallback: ESTIMATE — projected from micro-benchmark scores against a measured 8-core reference; real throughput depends on request mix, TLS ratio, upstream latency and load.

compare.title: VS NGINX COMPARISON
compare.desc: Head-to-head on this same host: throughput in three flavours — AEGIS's raw tokio serving stack, AEGIS with the real protection pipeline (WAF/filter engine) engaged per request, and an ephemeral nginx — all driven by the same load generator, plus a security matrix of real attacks AEGIS's WAF blocks that a vanilla nginx forwards straight to the origin.

compare.errorToast.title: Comparison error
compare.protectedNote: The "AEGIS + WAF" bar runs the real per-request inspection pipeline (full filter engine / WAF) before each response, so it includes the protection CPU cost — the honest price of defence, not the bare serving stack. Every target is driven by the same load generator over loopback.
compare.securityNote: Plain reverse proxies (nginx, HAProxy, Caddy, Envoy) ship no WAF — every one of these attacks is forwarded to the origin unmodified. AEGIS — and nginx+ModSec+CRS — block them with rule sets. This is the key differentiator.
